newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Khmer Rouge's Pol Pot on the run after defections.
newsitem.headline: Khmer Rouge's Pol Pot on the run after defections.

text.p: Reviled Khmer Rouge strongman Pol Pot was on the run in northern Cambodia after most of his remaining fighters deserted him, Cambodian officials said on Monday.
First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh said Pol Pot had fled toward the Thai border on Sunday in a convoy of 10 trucks, after reportedly slaughtering his defence chief and 11 family members.
He said six of the trucks were caught by Khmer Rouge guerrillas who had broken with their leader, the mastermind of Cambodia's 1975-79 "killing fields" reign of terror.
A senior Thai general, quoting intelligence reports, confirmed Pol Pot was on the run but said he did not expect the 69-year-old Maoist hardliner to flee towards Thailand.
Thailand and Cambodia have sealed their northern borders near Pol Pot's reported location.
Quoting Thai intelligence reports, General Jeerasak Promaprakorn, head of Thailand's task force bordering northern Cambodia, also said Pol Pot appeared to be seriously ill.
"My intelligence sources confirmed that he is in hiding in one of the mountains in northern Cambodia near the Thai border," Jeerasak told Reuters by telephone.

"I don't think that Pol Pot is heading in this (Thailand's) direction because he is not welcome here. But I think any action against him should also take into consideration humanitarian aspects because Pol Pot is badly sick," he said.
Ranariddh predicted Pol Pot's hardliners would be captured within two days. "This is the end of the Khmer Rouge...," Ranariddh said.

But Ranariddh appeared heading for a showdown with his co-Prime Minister Hun Sen over how to handle the disintegration of the guerrilla movement after Hun Sen warned that government officials who negotiated with the Khmer Rouge should be arrested.
Representatives of the co-premiers' parties met on Monday to discuss how to deal with the sensitive situation.
Co-Minister of Interior Sar Keng said after the meeting that Ranariddh's announcement that hardline rebels from the guerrilla's Anlong Veng base would join the government seemed premature.
Six divisions were ready to defect in Anlong Veng while two more remain loyal to Pol Pot, but the government needed more information on their intentions, Sar Kheng said.
Ranariddh had said about 95 percent of the guerrillas from Anlong Veng and a division led by Pol Pot, including four unidentified top officials, had decided to join the government.
Pol Pot was reported on Friday to have fled Anlong Veng after the guerrilla movement, already decimated by thousands of defections last August, split over whether to make peace with Phnom Penh.
The guerrillas reneged on a 1991 peace pact meant to end Cambodia's long history of conflict and have been fighting the coalition government formed after a U.N.-sponsored poll in May 1993.

Ranariddh said Pol Pot was holding senior figures hostage, including Khieu Samphan, president of the Khmer Rouge's provisional government, and added that rebel commander Ta Mok had broken with Pol Pot and disappeared.
Senior Thai general, Jeerasak, said his intelligence reports had indicated that Ta Mok was chasing Pol Pot.
Ranariddh said Briton Christopher Howes, abducted in March 1996 in Cambodia's northwest, was also in the group but could not say whether the British mine clearance expert was alive.
None of the reports about what is happening around Anlong Veng have been independently confirmed.
Many analysts wonder whether the entire episode may have been cooked up to distance the totally unpalatable Pol Pot from his marginally less despised comrades, who harbour some political aspirations.

In a surprise revelation, Ranariddh said he had met Khieu Samphan and two of his associates three weeks ago, but refused to provide details. Khieu Samphan recently said he hopes to form a political alliance with Ranariddh, a prospect the prince has welcomed.

The news of secret talks did not sit well with Hun Sen, who warned in a speech on local radio that anyone who negotiated with Khieu Samphan or other top rebels was breaking Cambodian law and would face arrest.
He demanded the Khmer Rouge leaders be arrested and brought to trial.
Relations between Ranariddh and Hun Sen, forced into an unhappy alliance by the U.N. elections in 1993, have deteriorated ahead of new polls due in 1998.
More than one million Cambodians died during the Khmer Rouge's disastrous experiment in total communism through executions, starvation, disease and hard labour.
"The Khmer Rouge is dead militarily, but someone wants the Khmer Rouge to survive politically. No way," Hun Sen said.
Hun Sen was part of the Vietnamese invasion force that eventually overthrew the Khmer Rouge regime and later led the Hanoi-backed government that ruled until 1991.
